lessons.title: What is a Forward Deployed Engineer?
objectives: Say in one sentence what an FDE does
Name the three skills the academy trains
Explain why mathematics comes first here

content.x: A Forward Deployed Engineer works directly with customers. When a bakery cannot trust its sales numbers, or a retailer wants an assistant that answers only from its own FAQ, an FDE sits with the people who understand the problem. They work out what mathematics and software can honestly deliver, build it, and explain it in plain language. The job is equal parts listener, modeller, builder and translator.

Many engineers rarely meet customers. An FDE is deployed to the edge — the customer's actual problem — which is why the role is named that way. It is a real, growing job family in consulting firms, product companies and AI teams, and it rewards exactly the skills this academy trains: careful mathematics, honest programming, and clear communication.

content.caption: The three skill layers and where the academy teaches them
rows: Turn a customer's story into numbers, rules and requirements
Write programs, clean data, connect APIs, deploy services
Document, demonstrate, and state limitations honestly

content.x: Why mathematics first? Because every later skill — programming, data, AI — quietly depends on it. A learner who can compute a break-even point and reason about a graph can learn any engineering tool. So Stage 2 is Foundation Mathematics, and it assumes nothing.

One habit matters more than talent here: verification. Every claim in this academy is checked — answers recomputed, outputs tested, demonstrations ticked against a checklist. You will practise that habit from your very first quiz.

lessons.title: The four operations, in real shops
objectives: Choose the right operation for a business question
Compute with confidence and check the result
Spot which operation a story problem is really asking for

content.x: Every business question about quantities uses one of the four operations. The skill is not computing — a calculator does that — it is knowing which operation the story is asking for. Addition brings quantities together ("144 rolls were baked, 57 sold — 201 handled so far"). Subtraction finds what remains or what changed. Multiplication repeats equal groups ("6 crates of 24 rolls"). Division shares or groups ("144 rolls into bags of 6").

content.caption: Story cues and the operations they signal
rows: shared equally, per box, each gets

content.x: Amara runs a market stall. On Friday she baked 144 rolls and sold 57 by noon. In the afternoon she sold rolls in bags of 6. A customer asks: "how many bags can I still buy, and how many rolls would be left over?" That is two operations in one story: first subtract to find what remains, then divide — and the remainder is the leftover rolls, not a rounding error to ignore.

steps.note: Subtract: rolls remaining after the morning.
The remainder answers the second half of the question.

lessons.title: Fractions you can see
objectives: Read a fraction as parts of a whole, not two separate numbers
Compare fractions using pictures and equivalents
Add fractions with the same denominator

content.x: A fraction names a part of a whole. In {3}/{4}, the bottom number (the denominator) says the whole was cut into 4 equal parts; the top number (the numerator) says we took 3 of them. The bar itself is the important part — it means "out of", not "divide whenever you feel like it".

Comparing fractions is easier when the parts are the same size. {2}/{4} and {1}/{2} shade the same amount — they are equivalent. To compare {2}/{3} with {3}/{4}, cut both wholes into 12: {8}/{12} against {9}/{12}, so {3}/{4} is bigger. Same denominator, compare tops; same top, compare bottoms (smaller bottom = bigger parts).

Adding fractions only works when the parts are the same size already: {2}/{5} + {1}/{5} = {3}/{5}. Amara sells {2}/{5} of her rolls before noon and another {1}/{5} by two o'clock — three fifths gone, two fifths left. When denominators differ, first rename both into a common one, then add tops.

content.prompt: Amara bakes one big tray. By 10am she has sold {1}/{4} of it, by noon another {2}/{4}. What fraction is left, and is that more or less than half?
content.hint: Same denominator — add tops, then compare with {2}/{4}.
content.solution: {1}/{4} + {2}/{4} = {3}/{4} sold, so {1}/{4} remains. A quarter is less than a half.

lessons.title: Decimals and money
objectives: Read decimals as fractions with power-of-ten denominators
Add and subtract money amounts without alignment mistakes
Round money honestly — up, down, and to the nearest

content.x: A decimal is a fraction wearing a different uniform: 0.25 is {25}/{100}, 0.5 is {5}/{10} is {1}/{2}. Money makes this concrete — £12.40 is twelve pounds and forty hundredths of a hundred pennies. The place values march by tens: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

The one rule that prevents most money mistakes: align the decimal points before adding or subtracting. 12.4 + 3.85 is a trap unless you write 12.40 + 3.85 = 16.25. Amara's till does this for her, but an FDE writing a script must do it for the till.

Rounding is a decision with consequences. Round £4.49 down to £4 for the business report and the month's totals drift by pennies that add up. The honest rule: say which way you rounded and why. "Nearest penny" is the default; "round up to whole items" appears whenever you cannot sell two-thirds of a roll.
Try the number line: place 4.49 between its neighbours and watch the nearest-hundredth snaps.

content.x: A ratio compares quantities in a fixed relationship. Amara's dough recipe uses flour and water in ratio 5 : 3 — five parts flour to three parts water. Double the flour and you must double the water; the relationship, not the raw numbers, is the rule. Scaling a recipe, an order or a delivery route is always this move: multiply every part by the same factor.

content.title: Scaling the recipe to 2 kg of flour

steps.note: Read the ratio as parts, not absolute weights.

content.x: The same arithmetic answers every "which is cheaper?" question. Shelf prices compare unfairly when pack sizes differ — a 300 g pack at £1.20 and a 500 g pack at £1.80 are only comparable through their unit price: price per 100 g. First pack: 120 ÷ 3 = 40p per 100 g. Second: 180 ÷ 5 = 36p per 100 g. The bigger pack wins, by 4p per 100 g — but only if you will actually use 500 g.

lessons.title: Percentages that mean something
objectives: Compute percentage of an amount, and percentage change, correctly
Read a percentage as a rate per hundred in context
Apply discounts and VAT-style markups with clear working

content.x: A percentage is a fraction with a promised denominator: "per hundred". 35% means {35}/{100} of whatever the whole is. The whole is the trap — "sales up 50%" can be honest and still tiny if the starting month was one bad week. Always ask: fifty percent of what?

Two everyday computations cover most business life. Percentage of an amount: 35% of 60 = 0.35 × 60 = 21 rolls sold in the morning rush. Percentage change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100 — if takings go from £240 to £300, that is 60 ÷ 240 = 25% up. Notice the change is always divided by the old value, not the new one.

steps.note: Subtract to get the final price.
Paying 80% of the original confirms the 20% off.

content.x: The distributive law says multiplication spreads over addition: a(b + c) = ab + ac. Going inward (expanding) turns a compact rule into a computable one: 3(2n + 4) = 6n + 12. Going outward (factorising) reveals structure: 6n + 12 = 6(n + 2), which says "three orders of (two rolls plus four)".

Why care about direction? Because questions ask different things. "What does one extra basket cost?" is easy from 6(n + 2) — six times the basket contents. "What is the cost for n = 5?" is easy from 6n + 12 — substitute and compute. Expanding exposes terms; factorising exposes structure. Engineers move both ways constantly.

lessons.title: Statements, and, or, not

content.x: A statement is a sentence that is definitely true or definitely false — never both, never neither. "The delivery arrived on Tuesday" is a statement. "Is the delivery here?" is a question; "deliver it soon" is a command; both are outside logic. Precision here is precision later: code conditions, database filters and AI refusals are all statements in costume.

AND demands both parts true; OR is satisfied by at least one (inclusive or); NOT flips. "Paid AND delivered" gates a shipment — one missing part blocks it. "Coupon OR member" grants the discount to either. "NOT damaged" passes only intact items.

lessons.title: If-then and the converse trap
objectives: Read if-then statements and spot when they are true

content.x: An if-then statement promises only one thing: IF the hypothesis holds THEN the conclusion does. "If the parcel weighs over 2 kg THEN it costs £6." The promise breaks only in one case: hypothesis true, conclusion false. A heavy parcel priced at £4 breaks it; a light parcel at £6 does not — the rule said nothing about light parcels.

The converse swaps the two parts, and it is a different claim. "If it costs £6 THEN it weighs over 2 kg" does not follow from the original rule — maybe £6 also covers bulky-but-light parcels. Swapping is how correct rules become incorrect ones; engineers who quote the converse without noticing ship bugs.
A counterexample kills a false claim with a single example: one £6 parcel under 2 kg disproves the converse instantly. Finding one is a superpower — it converts an argument into a fact.

lessons.title: Direct proof and proof by cases
objectives: Structure a direct proof: assumptions to conclusion

content.x: A direct proof walks from agreed facts to the conclusion with no leaps. Claim: "if a number of rolls n is even, then n² is even." Proof: even means n = 2k for some whole k; then n² = (2k)² = 4k² = 2(2k²), which is twice a whole number, hence even. Every symbol earned its place — that is the whole art.

Proof by cases handles claims that behave differently depending on the situation. Claim: "consecutive whole numbers always multiply to an even product." Cases: if the first is even, done; if the first is odd, the second is even, done. The cases cover everything — that exhaustiveness is what makes the proof complete. A proof with a gap ("what if the first is half-even?") proves nothing.
Why engineers prove things: a tested program shows the inputs you tried; a proof shows all inputs. Verification culture at the academy is the same idea at smaller scale — check, don't hope.

lessons.title: Sets, all and some
objectives: Read 'for all' and 'there exists' claims correctly

content.x: Two quantifiers run the world's claims. "For all" (∀) demands every case: "every delivery this week arrived on time." "There exists" (∃) demands just one: "some stallholder doubles prices on Saturdays." Getting these backwards is the classic specification bug.

Negation flips them: NOT(for all x, P(x)) = there exists an x where NOT P(x). "Not every delivery was on time" = "at least one delivery was late." You do not need every delivery to be late — one suffices. This one line of logic is why one failing test case breaks an "all tests pass" claim.

objectives: Decide what the nodes and edges should be

content.x: A graph is the honest minimal model of a connected situation: nodes for the things, edges for the direct relationships. Delivery routes: nodes are shops, edges are direct roads with their distances. Who-supplies-whom: nodes are businesses, edges are supply contracts. The modelling decision — what exactly becomes a node — is where most of the thinking happens.

A node's degree counts its edges. A shop with degree 1 sits on exactly one road: close that road and the shop is unreachable — no algorithm needed, just the definition. Degrees answer reachability questions the way arithmetic answers money questions: instantly and provably.

content.x: Finding the shortest path is greedy in the best sense: always expand the cheapest settled frontier. On our neighbourhood graph, from Stall to Bakery, brute force tries Stall→Market→Bakery (5 + 7 = 12) against Stall→Depot→Bakery (12 + 9 = 21) — the market route wins at 12 minutes. The method: keep a best-known distance to every node; improve it whenever a cheaper route appears; stop when your target is settled.

What the answer assumes: weights are trustworthy and stable (no Friday roadworks), and "shortest" means the weight you chose — minutes here, not kilometres or fuel. An FDE states this in the handover: shortest for whom, by which measure, as of when.

content.x: Connectivity asks: can every node reach every other? Trace it by hand on small graphs — follow edges, mark visited nodes, stop when nothing new is reachable. Any node left unmarked is genuinely unreachable, and no optimism changes that. This is the same flood-fill that powers image tools and, later in the academy, dependency checks.

Fragility has a shape: nodes of degree 1 hang off the network by a thread; nodes that all paths cross are single points of failure. Robustness means redundancy — a second road to the Café converts its closure from a disaster into a detour. Real infrastructure questions (payment fallbacks, deployment failovers) are this lesson with bigger numbers.

content.x: A flow network adds capacity to edges: how many boxes per hour can each road carry? The bottleneck is the narrowest point on any route — one 20-box road between two 60-box roads caps the whole chain at 20. Business pipelines behave identically: the oven, the packing line, the checkout — throughput of the chain is the throughput of its slowest edge.

The maximum flow from Stall to Bakery: 20 via Market, plus 30 via Depot = 50 boxes per hour total. The Market road could carry 60 but is fed only what the 20-cap road allows — widening the wrong road is the classic wasted investment. Find the bottleneck first; widen there.

lessons.title: Understand, plan, solve, check
objectives: Apply the four-step method to an unfamiliar problem

content.x: The method is four steps and one rule: never skip to step three. Understand: restate the problem in your own words, list what is given and what is asked. Plan: which tool fits — arithmetic, an equation, a graph, a table? Solve: execute the plan, carefully. Check: does the answer answer the QUESTION, is it plausible, can you verify it another way?

Worked example: "A market charges 30p per basket per hour, maximum 4 hours. Amara parks for 2.5 hours on Monday and 3 hours on Tuesday. What did she pay?" Understand: rate per hour, capped at 4; two days. Plan: compute each day separately, add. Solve: 2.5 × 30 = 75p; 3 × 30 = 90p; total £1.65. Check: both under the cap ✓; total more than either day ✓; recomputed once ✓.

The check step is where marks are saved in exams and where disasters are avoided in business. Half of all wrong answers fail only plausibility: a negative quantity, a 400% tip, a delivery route longer than the earth's circumference. Plausibility is free; install the habit.

content.x: A Fermi estimate answers "roughly how much?" by multiplying a few factors you can each defend. "How many loaves does our neighbourhood bakery sell weekly?" Break it: shops open 6 days; each day ~3 baking rounds; each round ~120 loaves; weekend demand ×1.3 on two days. 6 × 3 × 120 = 2,160, adjusted for weekend lift ≈ 2,400 loaves/week. The point is not precision — it is a sized answer in minutes, with every factor inspectable.

Estimates power real decisions: capacity planning ("can our single van cover 40 deliveries a day?"), staffing, stock. The discipline is the same three moves as this academy's projects: decompose, justify each factor, sanity-check the total against something known (e.g. the bakery's flour orders imply ~2,200 loaves — close enough).

content.x: A variable is a named box holding one value. In JavaScript: let price = 4.00; let rolls = 30; let takings = price * rolls;. The names do the remembering; the equals sign stores; the program computes left to right through the statements. Unlike the maths lesson, x does not get solved here — it gets used.

The sandbox on this page runs your code in an isolated worker — it cannot touch the page, your files or the network; it can only print to the output panel. That isolation is not decoration: it is the same principle the academy teaches about trust. Untrusted code runs in a cage; everything else stays safe.

The habit this stage installs is prediction-first: say what the program will print before pressing run. If reality disagrees with your prediction, the difference is the lesson — not a failure. Every lab below follows this loop: predict, run, compare.

content.x: Programs make choices with if statements: if (condition) { ... } else { ... }. The condition is a statement from the logic course — true or false, nothing between. Comparisons produce those statements: rolls > 100, takings === 60, customer !== member. Use === for equality (one = stores, three compares — mixing them is the classic beginner bug).

Boundary values are where bugs live. rolls > 100 is false at exactly 100 — is that the rule the customer wanted? "Above 100" and "100 or more" differ by one basket and one angry client. Trace branches by hand at the edges: 100, 101, 99. The trace costs thirty seconds; the bug costs a day.

content.x: A for loop repeats work: for (let i = 1; i <= 6; i++) { ... } runs the body six times with i = 1..6. The three parts are a contract: start here, keep going while this holds, step like this. Off-by-one bugs come from writing < when you meant <= — six crates need i <= 6, not i < 6.

The accumulator pattern (start a total at 0, add inside the loop) is the most-used loop shape in business code: totals, averages, counts. Its sibling the counter (start at 0, add 1 when a condition holds) answers "how many orders were over £50?" — a quantifier from the logic course, now executable.

content.x: A function wraps a computation behind a name: function breakEven(fixed, price, cost) { return Math.ceil(fixed / (price - cost)); }. The parameters are the slots; return hands the answer to whoever called. Printing shows a human something; returning gives the program something to use. They are different jobs.

Notice the guard: when contribution ≤ 0 the formula divides by zero or negative — the function returns Infinity honestly instead of a nonsense number. Functions are where business rules become reusable and testable: the same break-even logic from Stage 2, now callable on any vendor's numbers.

lessons.title: Why assistants hallucinate — and the grounding rule
objectives: Explain in plain language why language models invent facts
State the grounding rule this academy enforces on itself
Trace one grounded and one ungrounded answer

content.x: A language model predicts plausible text; it does not look up facts. Asked about your company's refund window, it will produce a fluent, confident, possibly invented answer — a hallucination. The failure is not stupidity; it is architecture. The fix is not better wording but better plumbing: give the model the sources and require the answer to come from them.

Retrieval searches a trusted corpus (your FAQ, your policy docs) for passages related to the question; grounding constrains the answer to those passages with citations. The academy's own rule — taught in Level 6 and enforced in the AI lab on this site — is: answer ONLY from retrieved sources with a citation; if retrieval finds nothing relevant, refuse and hand over to a human.

lessons.title: Build a tiny FAQ assistant (in the AI lab)
objectives: Explain keyword-overlap retrieval and its limits
Use the academy's AI lab against a real mini-FAQ
Recognise when to hand over to a human

content.x: You can build the core loop of a grounded assistant without any AI service: score questions by overlapping keywords, retrieve the best passage, and compose an answer that quotes it with a citation. The AI Lab's assistant on this site does exactly that over a small shop FAQ — retrieval you can read, grounding you can verify, refusals you can trigger.

Its honest limits: keyword overlap misses paraphrase ("money back" vs "refund"), and it knows nothing beyond its corpus. Those limits are the lesson — real systems add embeddings and re-ranking for the first problem and a human handover for the second. What never changes is the contract: sources in, citations out, refuse when unsure.

lessons.title: Handover: the human path is a feature
objectives: Design the handover path for an assistant demo
Write the honest-limits section for a handover document
Explain why 'production-ready' is earned, not declared

content.x: Every assistant ships with two paths: the automated one and the human handover. The handover triggers on refusal, on low retrieval scores, on complaints, and on anything touching money or safety. Far from being an admission of failure, it is the product working as designed — the same philosophy as the academy's projects: demos are demonstrations, with limits written down.

The handover document has four honest sections. What it does: grounded FAQ answers, with citations. What it does not: anything outside the corpus, or paraphrase beyond keyword overlap. How it fails: it refuses — visibly, with a path to a person. What would make it production-ready: a larger evaluation set, embedding-based retrieval, monitoring, and owner sign-off. Writing section four is the engineering maturity test.

Each bullet is checkable — that is what makes them engineering, not vibes.

books.title: Foundation Mathematics
books.subject: Mathematics
books.description: The complete beginner's mathematics textbook: from the four operations to break-even, every concept introduced through Amara's market stall and checked honestly.
objectives: Operate confidently with numbers, fractions, decimals and percentages
Model cost, revenue and break-even
Read tables and charts critically

content.x: Every business question about quantities uses one of the four operations: addition brings quantities together, subtraction finds what remains, multiplication repeats equal groups, division shares them out. The skill is recognising which one a story asks for — the story cues (in total, left over, each crate, shared equally) map directly onto +, −, × and ÷.

Amara's stall makes the abstractions concrete. 144 rolls baked, 57 sold by noon, bags of 6 in the afternoon: subtract to find what remains, divide to find full bags, and treat the remainder as real rolls rather than a rounding error. Remainders are where honesty lives in division.

content.prompt: 250 flyers in bundles of 8: how many complete bundles, how many left over?
content.hint: 250 ÷ 8, remainder honest.
content.solution: 31 bundles (248), 2 flyers remain.

content.x: A fraction names part of a whole: in {3}/{4} the denominator says the whole was cut into four equal parts and the numerator counts them. Comparisons need equal parts — rename into a common denominator and the tops decide. Decimals are the same fractions with power-of-ten denominators: 0.25 is {25}/{100}.

Money is the daily-life decimal. One alignment rule prevents most errors: line up the decimal points before adding or subtracting. 12.40 + 3.85 = 16.25, not 15.09 or whatever a misaligned column produces. Rounding is a decision: say which way and why — nearest penny, or up to whole items when fractions cannot be sold.

content.prompt: Add 12.4 + 3.85 + 0.05 with honest alignment.
content.hint: Two decimals everywhere.

content.x: A percentage is a fraction with a promised denominator: 35% = {35}/{100} of whatever the whole is. Percentage of an amount: 0.35 × 60 = 21. Percentage change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100 — always divided by the OLD value. A 20% discount then a 20% markup does not return to start, because the second 20% uses a smaller base.

content.prompt: £9.60 → £10.80: percentage increase?
content.hint: Change ÷ old.

chapters.title: Ratios, unit price and best buy

content.x: A ratio is a fixed relationship: 5 : 3 flour to water means every scaling multiplies both parts. Unit price makes different pack sizes comparable: price ÷ size, per 100 g. The offer that looks cheapest often is not — arithmetic is not fooled by pack sizing, and neither are you now.

content.prompt: 300 g at £1.20 vs 500 g at £1.80 — which is cheaper per 100 g?
content.hint: Divide by 3 and by 5.
content.solution: 40p vs 36p per 100 g — the bigger pack wins.

content.x: Break-even is where money in equals money out: fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit, where contribution = price − variable cost. £20 stall fee, £4 price, £1.50 cost → £2.50 contribution → 8 rolls. Round up to whole items; state what the model assumes (stable prices, everything sells, one product). A model that hides its assumptions gets trusted once too often.

content.prompt: Coffee cart: fixed £45, price £2.80, variable £1.05 — break-even cups?
content.hint: Contribution £1.75.

content.x: Tables are questions waiting to be asked. Read critically: what are the units, what is missing (a Sunday row?), what could be a confounder (market days vs rain)? Build the comparison that answers the actual question — weekday mean against market-day mean — instead of reciting raw numbers.

A chart is an answer, not a decoration. Trend over time → line; comparison across categories → bar; part-of-whole → fraction bar or pie. If you cannot say which question a chart answers, it does not go in the report. This chapter's rule applies to every dashboard in the academy.

The closing chapter combines everything: scale a recipe by ratio, price a discount honestly, compute the break-even for a new product line, and present the week in one table and one chart — each answering a stated question. Complete it, then take the Stage 2 topic test in the Assessment Centre.

books.title: Algebra: From Expressions to Quadratics
books.subject: Mathematics
books.description: Letters that stand for numbers: expressions, equations, straight lines and quadratics — each motivated by a business question.
objectives: Build expressions from word rules
Solve linear equations with balance reasoning
Read and interpret line and quadratic graphs

content.x: Algebra begins when a rule is too general for one number: takings = p × n. Letters are slots; substitution fills them; collecting like terms tidies. 3n + 2n = 5n, but 3n + 2 stays put — rolls and pounds do not merge.

content.prompt: Van cost: £40 + £2 per basket. Expression and value at 12 baskets?

content.x: The distributive law a(b + c) = ab + ac works both directions: expanding exposes terms for computing, factorising exposes structure for reasoning. 6n + 12 = 6(n + 2) says 'per-basket structure' in one glance.
An equation is a balanced scale: the same legal move on both sides. 4n − 12 = 60 → 4n = 72 → n = 18, checked by substitution. The check is the verification habit made algebraic.

y = mx + c: m is the per-unit rate, c the start value. The profit line y = 2.5n − 20 crosses zero exactly at break-even — algebra and graphs are two views of one fact. Steeper gradient = faster growth per sale.
Two rules at once: where two lines cross, both are satisfied. Chapters 5–7 develop this for pricing decisions and capacity questions.
Quadratic patterns arise whenever area, projectile motion or squared scaling appears. Chapters 8–10 introduce x², its parabola, and the factorisations that solve it.
Some quadratics cross the axis twice, once, or never — and the discriminant tells you which before you solve. Real business models use this to decide when a target is reachable at all.
The closing assessment: model a second product's price and quantity with an equation, a line and a quadratic constraint, then defend every assumption.

books.title: Logic & Proof
books.subject: Mathematics
books.description: Statements, truth tables, implications and proof techniques — the reasoning layer behind reliable rules and code.
objectives: Write precise compound statements
Test claims with truth tables and counterexamples
Structure direct proofs and proofs by cases

content.x: A statement is definitely true or false. AND demands both, OR is satisfied by one, NOT flips. Truth tables compute combinations without guessing — four rows for two statements, and every business rule ('refund if receipt AND 30 days, OR VIP') decomposes into exactly such a table.

content.prompt: VIP customer, no receipt, day 45: refunded under the rule above?
content.hint: Evaluate both sides of the OR.
content.solution: Yes — right side of OR is true. The rule makes VIPs unconditional.

content.x: An implication promises: hypothesis true ⇒ conclusion true. It fails only when hypothesis holds and conclusion does not. The converse swaps the parts and is a DIFFERENT claim — quoting it un-noticed ships bugs. One counterexample kills a false claim instantly.
A direct proof walks from agreed facts to the conclusion with no leaps. Even n ⇒ even n²: write n = 2k, then n² = 2(2k²), twice a whole number, hence even. Every symbol earned its place.
Cases must be exhaustive to prove; counterexamples need only be single to disprove. Both are daily tools: exhaustive case analysis in rule design, single counterexamples in code review.

For-all claims demand every case; there-exists claims demand one. Negation flips them — one failing test breaks 'all tests pass'. This is why single counterexamples are decisive in verification culture.
The closing assessment: take a written refund policy, translate it to logic, build its truth table, find the unintended cases, and propose the repaired rule with proof.

books.title: Graphs & Networks
books.subject: Mathematics
books.description: Nodes, edges, shortest paths and flows: modelling roads, deliveries and infrastructure as networks you can reason about.
objectives: Model situations as graphs
Find shortest paths and explain assumptions
Judge reachability, fragility and bottlenecks

content.x: A graph models connected situations minimally: nodes for things, edges for direct relationships, weights for minutes or costs. A node's degree counts its edges — a degree-1 shop sits on one road, and closing that road makes it unreachable by definition, no algorithm required.

Shortest paths settle the cheapest frontier first and improve a node's best-known distance only when a strictly cheaper route appears. Stall→Bakery: 5+7 = 12 beats 12+9 = 21. 'Shortest' means the weight you chose — minutes, not kilometres — as of the day the weights were true.

Reachability is traced by marking connected nodes; anything unmarked is genuinely unreachable. Degree-1 nodes hang by a thread; nodes all paths cross are single points of failure. Redundancy — a second road — turns failures into detours.

Flow networks add capacities to edges; a chain moves no more than its narrowest edge. Max flow adds the separate routes' capacities: 20 via Market + 30 via Depot = 50. Widen the bottleneck first — widening anything else is a wasted investment.
Closing assessment: plan the week's deliveries — shortest routes, a redundancy fix, and the throughput analysis — as a written handover with stated assumptions.

books.title: Problem Solving
books.subject: Mathematics
books.description: A repeatable method for messy questions: understand, plan, solve, check — with estimation and honest tables.
objectives: Apply the four-step method under uncertainty
Estimate with defensible factors
Read and build answer-driven tables and charts

content.x: Never skip to step three. Understand restates the problem; plan picks the tool; solve executes carefully; check asks whether the answer answers the QUESTION and whether it is plausible. Plausibility is free — install the habit.

Real questions arrive with holes. Fix them with assumptions that carry their origin ('based on last month'), solve, and report sensitivity — how the answer moves if a key assumption changes. Defensible beats confident.
Rough answers from justified factors: open days × rounds × loaves per round, adjusted, then sanity-checked against an independent quantity. Sized answers in minutes, every factor inspectable.
Read tables for units, missing rows and confounders; build comparisons that answer the actual question. Correlation is visible; cause is not — say so.
The stage closes with Mock Exam A in the Assessment Centre: four multi-part problems under time, each graded against the four-step method.

books.subject: Projects

objectives: Turn a customer story into a working artefact
Verify work against a rubric before claiming it
Document honestly for handover

content.x: Every project is a customer story with an artefact: read the brief, close knowledge gaps through linked lessons and labs, build along the steps, verify against the demonstration checklist, and submit for rubric scoring. Pass at 16/24 with no dimension below 2 — Understanding, Correctness, Craft, Safety, Operation, Communication. Passing adds the project to your portfolio and unlocks the next level.

P1.1 The Market-Stall Budget (spreadsheet): Amara's costs, prices and break-even, with formulas recomputed by hand. P1.2 The Delivery-Route Logic Pack: five route decisions argued with logic-table rigour. Both Level 1 projects demand honest arithmetic and a one-page assumptions table.

Expense tracker and sales-report automator (Level 2), dataset cleaning and a reporting database (Level 3), a task-tracker API and a feedback dashboard (Level 4). Each project ships with starter code, a dirty dataset or an API spec, and testing instructions whose expected outputs are stated — no 'it should look right'.

Package and ship, then operate with monitoring (Level 5). The FAQ assistant and document search with evaluation sets (Level 6). Level 7's simulated engagements change requirements mid-build and grade the handover as heavily as the code — because that is the job.

A rubric rewards what employers check: understanding, correctness, craft, safety, operation and communication. Demos are never called production-ready; handovers state limits. This chapter is the culture of the academy in eleven pages.

glossary.simple: An engineer who works at the customer's edge
glossary.detailed: An engineer embedded with customers: listens to the business problem, models it, builds the software/data solution, and explains it in plain language. Contrasts with engineers who rarely meet customers.
glossary.example: When a bakery cannot trust its sales numbers, an FDE sits with the owner, models the data flow, builds the cleaning script, and hands over documentation.

glossary.detailed: The habit of confirming a result by recomputation, testing, or a checklist before relying on it. In this academy, progress counts only when verified.
glossary.example: Recomputing a break-even total by hand before sending the pricing email.

glossary.simple: One of the four arithmetic actions
glossary.detailed: Addition, subtraction, multiplication or division. Word problems signal which one: in total (add), left (subtract), each crate (multiply), shared equally (divide).
glossary.example: 'Shared equally among the stalls' signals division.

glossary.detailed: The amount left over when a division does not come out exact. In business contexts it is often a real quantity (leftover rolls), not noise to discard.
A way of naming parts of an equal partition: {a}/{b} means b equal parts, a of them taken. The bar means 'out of'.
glossary.example: Selling {3}/{5} of a tray means 3 of every 5 rolls.

glossary.detailed: Fractions that shade the same total ({2}/{4} and {1}/{2}). Rename by multiplying top and bottom by the same number.
Price divided by quantity, expressed per 100 g (or per item) so different pack sizes can be compared fairly.
A comparison like 5 : 3 meaning five parts to three parts; scaling multiplies every part by the same factor.
glossary.example: Flour : water = 5 : 3 — doubling flour requires doubling water.

glossary.simple: The value a percentage is taken of
glossary.detailed: In percentage change, the OLD value is the base: change ÷ old × 100. Using the wrong base is the classic percentage bug.
A fraction with denominator 100: 35% = {35}/{100} of the whole. Always ask 'percent of what?'

glossary.simple: Where money in equals money out
glossary.detailed: The sales level at which total revenue equals total cost: fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit. Selling beyond it earns contribution as profit.
glossary.example: £20 fee, £2.50 per roll → break-even at 8 rolls.

glossary.simple: Costs that do not vary with sales
glossary.detailed: Costs paid regardless of quantity sold (stall fee, rent). They set the height of the break-even hurdle.
The cost that scales with each item (ingredients, packaging).
glossary.example: £1.50 of flour and butter per roll.

glossary.detailed: What each sale adds toward covering fixed costs. Business viability starts with contribution, not price.
A combination of numbers, letters and operations with no equality claim: 40 + 2b. Evaluate by substitution.
glossary.example: Takings = 4n is an expression for n rolls at £4.

glossary.detailed: Replacing letters with values and computing in order.
Adding terms with identical letter parts: 3n + 2n = 5n; constants merge with constants; n and constants never merge.
a(b + c) = ab + ac. The engine behind expanding brackets — and, factorised, behind structure-spotting.
Rewriting a sum as a product: 6n + 12 = 6(n + 2). Reveals per-unit structure that expanded form hides.
A claim that two expressions are equal; solved by applying the same legal move to both sides, then verified by substitution.

glossary.simple: Rate of change of a line
glossary.detailed: In y = mx + c, how much y changes per one step of x: the per-unit rate in business stories.
glossary.example: Profit y = 2.5n − 20: gradient 2.5 = £2.50 per extra roll.

glossary.detailed: A sentence with a definite truth value; questions and commands are not statements. The atoms of rules and code conditions.
glossary.example: 'The order shipped on Monday' is a statement.

glossary.detailed: A AND B is true only when both are true. Gates shipments, refunds and permissions.
A OR B is true when at least one holds (inclusive or).
NOT A reverses A's truth value; over quantifiers it flips for-all into there-exists.
glossary.example: NOT 'all delivered on time' = 'at least one late'.

glossary.detailed: IF hypothesis THEN conclusion; false only when hypothesis holds and conclusion does not.
'If Q then P' — a different claim from 'If P then Q'; rarely follows automatically.
glossary.example: From 'heavy ⇒ £6' the converse '£6 ⇒ heavy' may be false.

glossary.simple: One case that kills a claim
glossary.detailed: A single example satisfying the hypothesis but breaking the conclusion. Decisive in reviews and tests.
glossary.example: A £6 parcel weighing 1 kg disproves '£6 ⇒ heavy'.

glossary.detailed: A derivation from agreed facts to the conclusion. Every symbol earns its place.
glossary.example: Even n ⇒ even n² via n = 2k.

glossary.detailed: Proving a claim by covering every possible situation. Valid only when the cases are exhaustive.
glossary.example: n even / n odd covers all whole numbers.

glossary.detailed: A claim about every member: 'all deliveries on time'. Negated by a single counterexample.
A claim that some member exists: 'some roll is gluten-free' needs just one.
Nodes represent entities, edges represent direct relationships, weights quantify them. The minimal honest model of connected situations.
glossary.example: Shops as nodes, roads as weighted edges.

glossary.detailed: A vertex: a shop, a person, a server. Choose nodes deliberately — the modelling decision is the thinking.
glossary.example: Each stall is a node in the market graph.

glossary.detailed: A connection between two nodes, optionally weighted with minutes, cost or capacity.
The number of edges at a node. Degree 1 hangs by a thread — its only link failing cuts it off.
The route minimising total weight, found by settling the cheapest frontier first and improving only on strictly better routes.
Whether every node can reach every other via open edges; traced by marking reachable nodes.
glossary.example: Closing Depot–Café cuts the Café off.

glossary.detailed: A node or edge whose failure disconnects parts of the network. Fixes add redundancy — a second route.
A graph whose edges carry maximum rates (boxes/hour, requests/sec). Chain throughput equals its narrowest edge.
The minimum-capacity edge on a route (or stage in a pipeline); the only place widening helps.
The sum of flows on separate routes, bounded by bottlenecks.
A rough estimate built by multiplying a few defensible factors, then sanity-checked against an independent quantity.
A premise adopted to proceed, carrying its origin. Defensible assumptions cite sources and report sensitivity.
glossary.example: Demand ≈ 140 based on last month's best Saturday.

glossary.simple: A named box for one value
glossary.detailed: let price = 4.0; stores a value under a name for later use. The program remembers so you do not have to.
if (condition) {…} else {…} picks a path; the condition is a statement from logic. Boundary values are where bugs live.
for (start; keep-going; step) repeats a body; the classic bug is off-by-one (< vs <=).
glossary.example: for (let i = 1; i <= 6; i++) runs six times.

glossary.detailed: Parameters in, return out. Functions make business rules reusable and testable.
console.assert(actual === expected, msg) reports a failure when reality disagrees with expectation. Tests enforce the verification habit.
Confident model output not grounded in real sources. Fixed by plumbing (retrieval + grounding), not wording.
Finding corpus passages related to the question to feed the answering step. Quality depends on matching (keywords vs embeddings).
glossary.example: FAQ §2.1 retrieved for a refund question.

glossary.detailed: The contract: answer ONLY from retrieved passages, cite them, refuse when nothing relevant is found. The academy enforces this on itself.
Scoring passages by shared words after normalisation. Inspectable and honest, but blind to paraphrase.
A fixed list of questions with expected behaviours (answer+section, or refusal), scored for groundedness, helpfulness and honesty.
glossary.example: 10 questions, 8 grounded — scoped to the set.

glossary.detailed: The documented path from automated to human, plus the limits document: what it does, does not, how it fails, and what production-readiness would require.
glossary.example: Refusal message offers a person, not a shrug.

glossary.simple: A chain of reasons that ends in a conclusion
glossary.detailed: In logic an argument is a sequence of statements — premises followed by a conclusion. It is valid when the conclusion must be true whenever the premises are true. One counterexample to a premise weakens the argument; logic is how you tell a sound argument from a persuasive-sounding one.
glossary.example: Premises: "Every stallholder who pays the fee may trade on Saturday" and "Amara paid the fee". Conclusion: "Amara may trade on Saturday." The argument is valid — if the premises are true, the conclusion must be.

codingExercises.title: Coding lab — the off-by-one trap
codingExercises.instructions: This loop SHOULD total six crates of 24 rolls (144) but prints 120. Fix it, then add a test that would have caught it.
hints: Count the iterations: crate takes 1..5. Six crates need <= 6.
codingExercises.solution:
for (let crate = 1; crate <= 6; crate++) { total = total + 24; }
console.assert(total === 144, "six crates of 24");
